title: Leveraging Fruit Fly and Zebrafish Multi-Omics in Decoding Pathological Networks for Parkinson’s Disease Translation
content: Parkinson’s disease (PD) is the second most common neurodegenerative disorder, affecting more than 8.5–10 million people worldwide. Despite decades of research, no disease-modifying therapy is currently available, and existing treatments primarily provide symptomatic relief. Therapeutic development is further hindered by the multifactorial nature of PD and the late emergence of clinical symptoms, which typically occur after substantial dopaminergic neuronal loss. A comprehensive understanding of the interconnected molecular networks underlying disease progression is therefore essential for identifying effective therapeutic strategies. Recent advances in multi-omics technologies have expanded our understanding of the genetic, molecular, and metabolic alterations associated with PD, however, integrating these diverse datasets to distinguish conserved pathogenic mechanisms from model- or context-specific responses remains challenging. Cross-species integration of multi-omics datasets from complementary non-mammalian models, particularly the fruit fly (Drosophila melanogaster) and zebrafish (Danio rerio), provides a systems-level approach for identifying conserved disease-associated networks. Comparative analyses reveal convergent molecular alterations across multiple interconnected pathological processes, highlighting the potential of these models to uncover conserved mechanisms of PD pathogenesis. Integration of these molecular networks through multimodal and computational approaches may further facilitate therapeutic target prioritization and establish a stepwise translational pipeline from high-throughput discovery in flies and zebrafish to validation in mammalian models and human studies. This review examines multi-omics findings from flies and zebrafish across four key pathophysiological processes in PD, including proteostasis disruption, mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, and neuroinflammation, and evaluates their potential for identifying conserved disease mechanisms and therapeutic targets.
